name: Rust
title: Rust (1.100 / 2024 edition)
lifecycleNote: 1.100.0, released 12 November 2026, is the current stable release

type.text: **Traits decouple without inheritance**: Interface + implementation separate
**Zero-cost abstractions**: Monomorphization prevents abstraction coupling to runtime cost
**Ownership prevents aliasing**: Can't have multiple mutable references, eliminates coupling
**Associated types in traits**: Decouple trait from concrete types
**The never type is stable**: `!` names a function that never returns, and `Infallible` is now an alias for it, so divergence is a type a signature can carry
**Orphan rules couple trait implementations**: Can't impl external trait on external type

construction.text: **Constructors are just functions**: `new()` is convention, not special
**Builder pattern zero-cost**: Type-state pattern at compile time
**No shared mutable state**: Construction can't couple to globals
**Drop trait separates cleanup**: Destruction logic separate from construction
**Collection order is unpinned**: the documentation states HashMap's order varies with a per-process random seed; the ordered BTreeMap is the opt-in

memory.text: **Ownership system prevents memory coupling**: Compiler prevents use-after-free and double-free at compile time
**No GC, no pauses**: Deterministic deallocation via RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, via the Drop trait)
**Lifetime tracking decouples**: References can't outlive referents
**Zero-cost abstractions for memory**: Box, Rc, Arc explicit about allocation strategy
**Custom allocators are stable**: The `Allocator` trait and the `*_in` constructors on `Box` and `Vec` move a custom allocation strategy from an ecosystem crate into the standard library
**No implicit copies**: Move semantics by default prevent accidental copying
**Reference cycles with Rc**: `Rc<RefCell<T>>` cycles require Weak to break
**Lifetimes can couple**: Complex lifetime constraints create dependencies between regions
**Unsafe blocks bypass memory-safety guarantees**: Can violate all guarantees, but explicit
`Rc<RefCell<T>>` cycles leak (the standard-library documentation names it); `Weak` is the discipline

error.text: **Result<T, E> makes errors explicit**: Can't ignore errors without `.unwrap()`
**`?` operator composes**: Error handling doesn't obscure logic
**No exceptions**: All errors in type system
**Panics are rare**: Explicit unwrap/expect, or Result

concurrency.text: **Ownership prevents data races**: Compiler enforces Send/Sync
**Async/await with explicit futures**: Concurrency in types
**Channels separate communication**: Message passing decouples concurrent tasks
**No shared mutable state without explicit synchronization**: Arc/Mutex make coupling visible

platform.text: **No vendor lock-in**: Compiles to native code for every major platform
**Broad target support**: Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, and bare-metal `no_std`
**Static linking by default**: A binary does not couple to a platform's runtime or shared libraries

**The target list keeps widening**: 1.99 promoted `riscv64-unknown-linux-musl` to Tier 2 with host tools, and 1.100 promoted `wasm32-wasip3` to Tier 2 and moved `i686-pc-windows-gnu` to Tier 2 without host tools

performance.text: **Compile-time optimization**: LLVM 23 backs the 1.100 compiler as it backed 1.99, so inlining and vectorisation arrive without a source change
**Binary size**: Can be large without optimization

ecosystem.text: **Smaller than JVM/npm**: Fewer libraries than established ecosystems
Crates ship source, and Rust-to-Rust binaries do not cross a producer boundary; exported symbols cross to C consumers on the platform ABI [@sysvAmd64Abi]
**Cargo has its own lint system**: the `[lints.cargo]` table controls the warnings cargo emits, and the built-in `cargo::unused_dependencies` lint is warn by default

evolution.text: **Editions system**: Breaking changes isolated to editions
**Async runtime**: Tokio is the de facto standard; async support has stabilized at the language level (2024 edition)

**An edition can change what existing code means (V1)**: Edition 2024 rewrote the capture rules of `impl Trait`, required `unsafe extern`, and reserved `gen`, so a crate that adopts it must be revisited

**The last three releases changed what existing code meets**: 1.98 turned some ambiguous glob imports into a hard error, 1.99 made `no_mangle_generic_items` a hard error and fully deprecated the legacy integral modules, and 1.100 changed the never type fallback from `()` to `!` on all editions
**Build variants multiply**: cfg attributes and cfg!(...) blocks select which items compile, and --cfg flags set the space

**Two Cargo defaults moved with no compiler error (V5)**: `cargo install` now uses the `Cargo.lock` shipped in the `.crate` tarball by default, so a deployment that names no dependency version receives the publisher's locked set instead of a fresh resolution and `--locked` is a no-op, and Cargo uses a new directory layout for intermediate build artifacts, so a tool that inspects the build directory for output silently breaks. Why: the Cargo team made install agree with the build, so the installed executable carries the dependency set the publisher tested, and the build layout is documented as a private interface, so Cargo re-laid it out without a deprecation cycle. How a deployment reverses it: pin the toolchain to a 1.99.x release in `rust-toolchain.toml` and both defaults return, or move artifact-lookup tools to Cargo's JSON messages, the documented stable interface. Both changes are recorded and neither is priced: the locked resolution is a gain in reproducibility and a delay of a security fix published after the tarball, and the layout change costs the inspecting tool and buys Cargo freedom, so the same presence has to mean a gain and a loss at once

domain.text: **Excellent for systems**: Memory safety without GC
**Strong for CLI tools**: Single binary, fast startup
**Backend less common**: Growing but smaller than Java/Go

learning.text: **Compiler fights you**: Borrow checker takes time to internalize
**Excellent docs**: The Book, Rustlings, error messages

testing.text: **Symbol names changed by default**: 1.97 made v0 mangling the default, so a debugger or profiler with an older demangler prints raw symbol names

security.text: **No null**: Option<T> prevents null pointer derefs
The release build wraps in two's complement (documented); the debug panic is a mitigation, priced

reproducibility.text: Cargo.toml is the contract cargo reads and validates, with the lockfile it writes.

supplychain.text: crates.io packages carry no signed provenance beyond TLS.
The crates.io name space is flat.
The RustSec Advisory Database is a community project, not a registry feed.

**Minimum publish age is available**: the `global-min-publish-age` setting makes the resolver ignore dependency versions published more recently than the set age unless they are already in `Cargo.lock` (RFC 3923), a supply-chain guard a deployment opts into

observability.text: No tracing standard ships with the language; the tracing crate is the ecosystem answer.
println! and the log facade carry no in-language structure.
A panic prints a backtrace only when RUST_BACKTRACE is set.

feedback.text: Monomorphization and crate graphs make release builds slow.

interop.text: extern blocks are the in-process C interface.
rustc targets every common triple, cross-compiling from one host.

governance.text: The Rust Foundation and the teams govern through a public RFC process.
rustc and the standard library are public source.

tradeoffs: **Safety vs. Flexibility**: Borrow checker rejects valid programs that don't fit ownership model
**Lifetime Complexity**: Memory safety without GC vs. lifetime bounds coupling function signatures to their callers
**Trait Coherence vs. Modularity**: Orphan rules prevent implementing external traits on external types
verdict: Rust's design yields exceptionally low language-imposed coupling. The ownership system prevents aliasing and use-after-free at compile time. Result types make errors explicit and composable. Traits decouple interface from implementation without inheritance. Concurrency safety is enforced by the compiler through Send and Sync. Main strength: the compiler detects coupling that other languages defer to runtime. Main weakness: the learning curve is real, and complex lifetime constraints couple function signatures to their callers' contexts.

energy.text: Compiles to native code: the fastest class in the language energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy; @pereira2021ranking]. A causal re-analysis attributes the difference to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: A standards-qualified toolchain or an established safety standard covers this language.

delivery.note: A crate ships source, and cargo compiles it with the toolchain in use
An rlib records the compiler release that built it, and no consumer outside that build links one
Exported symbols cross to other code on the platform's published C ABI
